sections.title: Overview
sections.subtitle: What Kuya is, in business terms and in engineering terms
sections.business_pov:
Data teams at Acme were losing **three engineer-days a week** to babysitting cron jobs that failed silently. Kuya replaces that with a declarative scheduler: you describe the work, Kuya guarantees it runs, retries on failure, and reports what happened.

The business outcome is boring and valuable — dashboards are correct by 6am, and nobody gets paged for a transient S3 timeout.

analogies.title: The restaurant ticket rail
analogies.body: Imagine a busy kitchen. Orders come in and get clipped to a rail above the pass. Each station — grill, sauce, plating — only starts when the one before it hands the plate along. Nobody has to shout; the rail is the contract. In Kuya, your functions are the stations, and the rail is a **DAG (directed acyclic graph)** — a map of what has to finish before the next thing can start.

analogies.title: The persistent sous chef
analogies.body: Now suppose the grill station has a bad night and burns a steak. A good sous chef doesn't abandon the order — they retry it, note what went wrong, and keep the kitchen running. Kuya's **scheduler** does exactly this: it holds **run history** in a database (PostgreSQL), re-attempts failures with a back-off, and surfaces the result in a dashboard so the head chef (you) can see every ticket that was ever fired.

analogies.title: Separating the menu from the kitchen
analogies.body: The restaurant owner writes the menu (what dishes to make, in what order). The kitchen staff execute it. Kuya makes the same split: you write **task definitions** in Python, and a pool of **executors** (worker processes) runs them in parallel. Adding more executors is like hiring more line cooks — the menu stays the same, the throughput goes up.

notes: Kuya is **not** a stream processor — if your latency budget is under a second, use the event bus instead.
The scheduler is single-writer by design; horizontal scale comes from executors, not from running two schedulers.
Losing Redis loses queued work but never run history — Postgres is the source of truth.

blocks.title: Where Kuya fits
blocks.text: Kuya sits between your orchestration triggers (cron, CI, webhooks) and your compute. It does not transform data itself — it sequences and retries the functions that do.

sections.title: Your first pipeline
sections.subtitle: Fifteen minutes, one file, one scheduled task.
sections.body:
## 1. Install dependencies

```bash
uv add kuya
```

This pulls the Kuya SDK and its CLI into your virtual environment.

## 2. Initialise a project

```bash
uv run kuya init
```

Writes a `kuya.toml` (scheduler config) and a `pipelines/` directory with a sample task.

## 3. Write your first task

```python
from kuya import task, pipeline

@task(retries=3, timeout="5m")
def fetch_orders(day: str) -> str:
    return f"s3://raw/orders/{day}.parquet"

@task
def summarise(path: str) -> int:
    return count_rows(path)

@pipeline(schedule="0 5 * * *")
def daily_orders(day: str):
    return summarise(fetch_orders(day))
```

Two things to notice: `retries` is declared on the task, not coded inside it. And `daily_orders` returns the *last* task — Kuya infers the DAG from the Python call graph.

## 4. Run it locally

```bash
uv run python quickstart.py
```

You should see two task records appear in the local scheduler UI at `http://localhost:8080`.

## 5. Deploy to staging

```bash
uv run kuya deploy --env staging
```

Deployment is a no-op if the DAG hash is unchanged, so it is safe to run in CI on every merge.

sections.title: How it works
sections.subtitle: Control plane, data plane, and how they talk to each other.

blocks.text:
From the outside, you write Python functions and decorate them. From the inside, there are two planes that never share code:

- **Control plane** — decides *what* runs and *when*.
- **Data plane** — decides *where* and actually executes your code.

blocks.title: Upgrade order matters
blocks.text: Migrate PostgreSQL first, then roll executors, then roll the scheduler. Rolling the scheduler first will enqueue work in a format old executors cannot read.

blocks.title: Failure modes worth knowing
items: An OOM-killed executor leaves its run row in RUNNING until the lease expires (10 minutes by default).
A PostgreSQL failover pauses scheduling but loses no run history.
Redis eviction drops queued work; the scheduler re-enqueues on the next tick.

blocks.title: Minimal Helm values
blocks.text:
scheduler:
  replicas: 1
executor:
  replicas: 6
  resources:
    limits:
      memory: 4Gi
postgres:
  external: true
  dsn: ${KUYA_DSN}

decks.name: Core concepts
decks.description: The vocabulary you need before reading any Kuya pipeline.

cards.back: A **directed acyclic graph** — tasks are nodes, dependencies are edges, and no path loops back on itself. Kuya infers it from your function call graph.
Kuya will re-invoke the task up to three more times on failure, with exponential back-off. It does **not** guarantee the task is safe to re-run — that is your job.
cards.hint: The scheduler promises attempts, not correctness.

cards.back: Because retries and backfills re-run the same task with the same inputs. If the task appends instead of overwriting, a retry silently doubles your data.
PostgreSQL. Redis only carries in-flight work hand-off to executors, so losing Redis costs you queued work but never run history.
cards.hint: Think: which store survives a Redis flush?

cards.back: Re-running a pipeline over a historical range of schedule intervals — typically after fixing a bug or adding a new task to an existing DAG.

decks.name: Operating Kuya
decks.description: What you need when something is on fire at 3am.

cards.front: A task is stuck in RUNNING with no logs. First check?
cards.back: Whether its executor pod still exists. An OOM-killed executor leaves the run row in RUNNING until the lease expires (default 10 minutes).

cards.front: How do you stop a runaway pipeline immediately?
cards.back: Pause the pipeline, then cancel in-flight runs. Pausing alone does not stop work already handed to an executor.
cards.code:
kuya pipeline pause daily_orders
kuya run cancel --pipeline daily_orders --state running

cards.front: Two schedulers are running. What happens?
cards.back: The second one fails to acquire the Postgres advisory lock and exits. The scheduler is single-writer by design — scale executors instead.

decks.name: Common pitfalls
decks.description: Mistakes that are easy to make and painful to debug.

cards.front: You added a new task to a running pipeline. What do you need to do?
cards.back: Redeploy (`kuya deploy`). The DAG hash changes and the scheduler picks up the new shape on the next tick. In-flight runs of the old DAG shape will complete normally.

cards.front: You upgraded the scheduler before migrating Postgres. What breaks?
cards.back: The scheduler writes new run rows in the upgraded schema; old-version executors cannot parse them and will crash or skip work. Always migrate Postgres first.

quizzes.name: Kuya basics
quizzes.description: Covers the overview, your first pipeline, and how it works.

questions.prompt: How does Kuya determine the shape of a DAG?
choices: From a YAML file you maintain by hand
By inferring it from the function call graph inside @pipeline
By scanning the database for prior runs
It asks the scheduler at runtime
questions.explanation: The `@pipeline` function body is traced; calling `summarise(fetch_orders(day))` is what creates the edge between those two tasks.

questions.prompt: Which of these are stored in PostgreSQL rather than Redis?
questions.explanation: Redis carries only the ephemeral hand-off to executors. Everything durable — run history, scheduler state, retry counts — lives in Postgres.

questions.prompt: Declaring `retries=3` makes a task safe to re-run.
questions.explanation: It makes the task *retried* up to three times; it does nothing to make the task *idempotent*. Retry-safety is a property of your code, not of the decorator.

questions.prompt: Running two scheduler instances doubles throughput.
questions.explanation: The second scheduler cannot acquire the Postgres advisory lock and exits immediately. Scale executors instead of schedulers.

questions.prompt: A task is stuck in RUNNING with no logs. What is the most likely cause?
choices: A network partition between scheduler and Postgres
The executor pod was OOM-killed and the lease has not yet expired
questions.explanation: An OOM-killed executor leaves the run row in RUNNING until the lease expires (10 minutes by default). Check whether the pod still exists first.

questions.prompt: Which component is intentionally limited to a single running instance?
questions.explanation: The scheduler is single-writer by design; it holds a Postgres advisory lock. The API and executors can all be replicated freely.

questions.prompt: What is lost if Redis goes down completely?
choices: Only work that was queued but not yet picked up by an executor
Nothing — Kuya falls back to Postgres for the queue
questions.explanation: Redis holds only in-flight work hand-off. The scheduler re-enqueues any lost work on its next tick. Postgres remains the source of truth.

questions.prompt: When you add a new task to an existing pipeline, which of these steps are required before it runs in production?
choices: Run a backfill if you need historical data
questions.explanation: `kuya deploy` is required — it pushes the new DAG hash to the scheduler. A backfill is needed only if you want the new task to run over past dates. Executor pods and pause/resume are not required.

questions.prompt: In the correct upgrade sequence, what comes first?
questions.explanation: Migrate Postgres first, then roll executors, then roll the scheduler. Rolling the scheduler first enqueues work in a format old executors cannot read.

questions.prompt: `kuya deploy` is safe to run on every CI merge even if nothing changed.
questions.explanation: Deployment is a no-op when the DAG hash is unchanged, so running it on every merge is intentional and safe.
